questions.q: What are the two interchangeable Snowflake syntaxes for an auto-generated sequential key column?
options: PRIMARY and UNIQUE
AUTOINCREMENT and IDENTITY
SEQUENCE and SERIAL
HASH and MD5
questions.explain: Snowflake supports both AUTOINCREMENT and IDENTITY(1,1)-style syntax, with the same underlying behavior — mirroring T-SQL's IDENTITY concept.

questions.q: Why aren't Snowflake AUTOINCREMENT values guaranteed to be gap-free or in strict insertion order?
options: Only VARCHAR columns can use AUTOINCREMENT
Snowflake loads data in parallel across many micro-partitions, so concurrent inserts don't guarantee sequential, gap-free assignment
Snowflake resets the counter to zero after every query
AUTOINCREMENT is not actually supported in Snowflake
questions.explain: Because loading happens in parallel across micro-partitions, values assigned by concurrent inserts can have gaps or arrive out of insertion order, more pronounced than T-SQL's IDENTITY.

questions.q: What does a HASH()-based surrogate key pattern compute the key from?
options: The natural/business key, deterministically, right inside the transformation that builds the dimension
A random number generated fresh on every insert
The current system timestamp only
The row's physical storage location in the micro-partition
questions.explain: HASH(customer_id) (or similar) derives the surrogate key deterministically from the natural key, so the same input always produces the same key.

questions.q: Why does a HASH()-based key avoid needing a 'round trip' that AUTOINCREMENT requires?
options: HASH() keys are only used for VARCHAR columns
It can be computed independently by any transformation that knows the natural key, without first inserting into the dimension and reading back the assigned value
AUTOINCREMENT cannot be used in any SELECT statement
HASH() values are always smaller than AUTOINCREMENT values
questions.explain: A fact table transformation can compute HASH(customer_id) itself to match a dimension's key without waiting on an INSERT-and-read-back cycle against the dimension table.

questions.q: Why does a HASH()-based key survive a CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT rebuild more cleanly than AUTOINCREMENT state?
options: HASH() keys are stored outside the table so rebuilding never affects them
AUTOINCREMENT columns are deleted whenever a table is replaced
It's recomputed identically every time from the same natural key, whereas AUTOINCREMENT state isn't preserved automatically across a full table rebuild
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE AS SELECT is incompatible with AUTOINCREMENT columns and will always error
questions.explain: Because a HASH()-based key is deterministic and recomputed from source data every run, it naturally matches across rebuilds, while AUTOINCREMENT's internal counter state isn't guaranteed to line up the same way after a full CREATE OR REPLACE rebuild.
